q: How do you separate cool-climate Syrah from Grenache blind?
accept: pepper olive violets savory versus raspberry alcohol warmth pale
syrah rotundone grenache alcohol
ans: Syrah: rotundone pepper, olive, cured meat, deeper color, medium+ tannin. Grenache: paler rim, raspberry-strawberry, garrigue, higher alcohol warmth, softer tannin
exp: In a GSM the pepper says Syrah's share; the heat says Grenache's.

q: Distinguish Sauvignon Blanc's three homes blind: Marlborough, Sancerre, Bordeaux.
accept: marlborough passionfruit thiol sancerre flint grapefruit bordeaux oak semillon waxy
nz tropical loire mineral bordeaux barrel
ans: Marlborough: passionfruit-thiol explosion, riper. Sancerre: grapefruit, flint, chalky restraint. Bordeaux: oak/lees texture, Sémillon's wax, lower aromatic pitch
exp: Riper thiols = New World; flint = silex; wax = a blending partner.

q: What structural evidence would push a white call toward Austria over Germany?
accept: dry higher alcohol white pepper lentil versus lower alcohol residual sugar petrol
gruner pepper dry versus riesling rs
ans: Bone-dry finish at 12.5–14%, white pepper/lentil (Grüner) or dry stone-fruited Riesling — versus Germany's lower alcohol and frequent residual sugar
exp: Alcohol level is the fastest Germany/Austria discriminator.

q: What does bruised apple, sherry-like nuttiness and a browning rim in a young white tell you, and what is your professional response?
accept: oxidation fault reject bottle check others
oxidized wine replace and check the case
ans: Premature oxidation — a fault: pull the bottle, check other bottles from the case, notify the supplier
exp: Distinguish deliberate oxidative styles (Jura, Sherry) from accidental death.

q: Two glasses of Chardonnay: one Chablis, one Meursault. Give three discriminating markers.
accept: acid higher chablis oyster shell lean meursault hazelnut oak richer body
chablis leaner meursault richer
ans: Chablis: higher acid, oyster-shell/lemon, little to no oak, leaner body. Meursault: hazelnut-butter, oak-lees richness, riper orchard fruit, broader mouthfeel
exp: Beware oaked Chablis grand cru — then judge acid line and fruit ripeness.

q: Explain wine's four principal phenolic groups and where each lives.
accept: anthocyanins skins tannins seeds skins stems flavonols skins stilbenes resveratrol
anthocyanin tannin flavonol stilbene
ans: Anthocyanins (skins, color), tannins/proanthocyanidins (seeds, skins, stems), flavonols like quercetin (sun-exposed skins), stilbenes like resveratrol
exp: Seed tannin is harsher; skin tannin rounder — hence extraction decisions.

q: Explain what actually changes in a red wine as it ages — colour, tannin and aroma.
accept: anthocyanins polymerize with tannin colour fades tannin softens then precipitates and fruit gives way to tertiary aromas
pigmented polymers form tannin chains grow and drop out esters hydrolyse
colour browns tannin softens and precipitates primary fruit becomes tertiary
slow oxygen ingress drives polymerization and tertiary development
the tannin polymerizes into long chains and leaves the wine as sediment
ans: Colour: free anthocyanins are unstable and either bond with tannin into pigmented polymers or fall out of solution, so the wine moves purple to ruby to garnet, browning at the rim, and the sediment is the pigment leaving. Tannin: monomers polymerize into longer chains, which changes how they bind salivary protein and so reads as softening — then the chains grow too large to stay in solution and precipitate, which is why a very old wine can taste hollow. Aroma: fermentation esters hydrolyse and primary fruit fades, while slow reactions fed by the small oxygen budget entering through the closure build tertiary notes — forest floor, truffle, dried fruit, leather, tobacco. The whole process is oxygen management: too much and it is oxidation, too little and the wine reduces.
exp: Two points an examiner listens for. First, softening and sediment are the same process at two stages — the tannin did not disappear, it left the glass, which is why over-aged wines lose structure rather than gain finesse. Second, ageing is a function of oxygen, not of time: the same wine under a tin-lined screwcap, under a graded DIAM and under natural cork will be three different wines at fifteen years, and cellar temperature changes the rate again. Add the detail that pigmented polymers are far more stable to pH and SO2 than free anthocyanins, which is why a mature red's colour, once garnet, then changes very slowly.

q: Coravin's mechanism and its known limits:
accept: argon needle through cork sparkling no old crumbly corks risk
teflon needle argon pressure not for sparkling
ans: A needle through the cork pours under argon; limits: sparkling (dedicated model aside), fragile old corks, wax capsules, synthetic closures
exp: BTG economics changed; know the failure modes.

q: 'Négociant micro-labels' in Burgundy's shortage era mean:
accept: small merchants buying grapes lucien le moine benjamin leroux
micro-negoce model grape purchase top crus
ans: Micro-négoce (Benjamin Leroux, Lucien Le Moine, etc.) buying tiny grand-cru lots — merchants outperforming some domaines
exp: The domaine/négoce quality line dissolved this century.

q: Explain 'allocation tiering' as practiced by cult lists.
accept: purchase history loyalty tiers offers
buy history determines future access
ans: Purchase history builds tier status; loyalty buys access to the scarcest lots — the list is the market
exp: Restaurant somms trade on allocations the public can't touch.

q: How do you authenticate a suspicious bottle of old Burgundy? Give five checks.
accept: provenance chain glass mold label print cork branding fill capsule ullage
paper trail bottle glass label printing cork
ans: Chain of provenance; bottle glass and mold seams for period accuracy; label printing/paper aging; cork branding and length; fill level and capsule consistency — then the estate's own records
exp: Kurniawan was caught by paper and glass, not by taste.

q: Explain 'in bond' storage and its two commercial advantages.
accept: duty tax deferred provenance guarantee resale
bonded warehouse no duty until release
ans: Wine held in a bonded warehouse with duty and VAT deferred until release — cheaper to trade and a documented provenance trail for resale
exp: The fine-wine investment market runs almost entirely in bond.
